messages.body_plain:
I am looking at using the posterior sampler as an alternative to getting fitted values from the model, because adding the prediction set with the output variable set to NA can sometimes stress INLA for larger prediction sets. As I see it, this would involve (1) calling every predictor in the model (as opposed to just some) and (2) using rnorm as appropriate when new levels of a latent group are encountered (e.g., new levels of a random effect, akin to allow.new.levels of lme4).  Is there a straightforward way to do this without specifying each individual predictor in the model?

Many thanks,

Jonathan

messages.subject: Is there a legitimate shortcut for computing post-hoc linear combinations that doesn't involve enormous posterior samples?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a legitimate shortcut for computing post-hoc linear combinations that doesn't involve enormous posterior samples?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a 'besag' spatially varying regression coefficient model working pretty well. The model estimates an annual response over 60 years over 600 aerial units. I need to save 10,000 posterior samples per year and per aerial unit to do post-hoc aggregation (linear combinations) of results -- that's 60 x 600 x 10,000 = 360 million samples. I have to repeat this modeling exercise 550 times, and all this is stressing my computing resources. So I am looking for shortcuts for post-hoc aggregation (linear combinations),so I don't have to produce and save all these enormous posterior sample files.

I am hoping, for a given model, that rather than saving 360 million samples, I can save 60 x 600 x 2 (mean and SD) = 72 thousand posterior summaries. Then use these posterior summaries with rnorm() to recreate something like faux posterior samples for use in computing post-hoc aggregations (linear combinations). I have also messed around with trying to get something like a simplistic version of the Delta Method (summing variances) to work here, but am not happy with how that is going. Monte Carlo simulation seems more straight forward.

But here is the problem, when I compute post-hoc aggregate estimates over aerial units using the summaries in a Monte Carlo approach, the confidence intervals are considerably smaller than when I do it with the standard approach using true posterior samples. I imagine that this is due to the Monte Carlo approach not incorporating all sources of uncertainty. Or maybe I just coded it wrong?

Does any of this make sense? If so, do you have any feedback? If it is not clear what I am talking about, and you are mildly intrigued or bored, I pasted R code for a reproducible example, below.

Thanks for any insight.

Best,
Tim

# ******************************* set up ***************************************
# load libraries
require(spdep)
require(spatialreg)
require(sf)
require(ggplot2)
require(dplyr)
require(INLA)

# set some simulated data parameters
rows <- 20; cols <- 20; cells <- rows*cols; yrs <- 10
intercept <- 10; rand_ints <- sort(runif(cells, -3, 3))
rand_slopes <- sort(runif(cells, -1, 1)); cv <- 0.2

# make a grid cell map and plot it
sf1 <- st_polygon(list(rbind(c(-108,36), c(-106,36), c(-106,38),
                             c(-108, 38), c(-108,36))))
grid1 <- st_make_grid(sf1, n=cols) %>%
  st_cast(to="POLYGON") %>% st_sf() %>%
  mutate(id=as.numeric(row.names(.)))
st_crs(grid1) <- 4326; plot(grid1); grid1

# make a time series PER grid cell and plot a few time series
dat1 <- expand.grid(id=grid1$id, yr=1:yrs) %>%
  arrange(id, yr)
z <- c()
for(i in unique(dat1$id)){
  yr <- 1:yrs
  y <- intercept + rand_ints[i] + rand_slopes[i]*yr +
    rnorm(yrs, 0, (intercept+rand_ints[i])*cv)
  z <- c(z, y)
}
dat1 <- dat1 %>% mutate(z=z, random_ints=id, random_slopes=id)
ggplot(data=subset(dat1, id==1|id==150|id==250|id==350), aes(x=yr, y=z)) +
  geom_point() + facet_wrap(~id, scales="free") + geom_smooth(method="lm")

# make neighborhood weights from grid map
nb1 <- poly2nb(grid1, row.names=grid1$id); nb1
weights1 <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(nb2listw(nb1)), "CsparseMatrix")

# make spatially varying coefficient model formula
form1 <- z ~ 1 +
  f(random_ints, model="besag", graph=weights1, constr=T, scale.model=T) +
  f(random_slopes, yr, model="besag", graph=weights1, constr=F, scale.model=T)

# call inla and view results
inl1 <- inla(form1, data=dat1, control.compute=list(config=T))
summary(inl1); plot(inl1)
grid1$rand_slopes_mean <- inl1$summary.random$random_slopes$mean
grid1$rand_slopes_sd <- inl1$summary.random$random_slopes$sd
plot(grid1["rand_slopes_mean"])
plot(grid1["rand_slopes_sd"])

# select and map a grid cell subset of interest for post-hoc aggretation
subset <- 1:200
plot(grid1[subset, "rand_slopes_mean"])
plot(grid1[subset, "rand_slopes_sd"])

# get a bunch of posterior samples for model parameters
inla.posterior.sampler <- function(result=inl1,
                                   full.ss=1000,
                                   part.ss=500,
                                   exclude_random="overdisp"){
  out <- c()
  n.loops <- full.ss / part.ss
  all.par.names <- row.names(as.data.frame(
    inla.posterior.sample(1, result)[[1]]$latent))
  fix_samp_names <-row.names(result$summary.fixed)
  fitted_samp_names <- gsub(pattern="fitted.", replacement="",
                            row.names(result$summary.fitted.values))
  fitted_samp_names <- gsub("(?<![0-9])0+", "", fitted_samp_names, perl = TRUE)
  fitted_samp_names <- gsub(pattern=".", replacement=":", fitted_samp_names,
                            fixed=T)
  random_samp_names <- names(result$summary.random)[names(
    result$summary.random)!=exclude_random]
  for(i in 1:n.loops){
    post.1 <- inla.posterior.sample(part.ss, result)
    post.2 <- as.matrix(sapply(post.1, function(x) x$latent))
    block.1 <- t(post.2)
    colnames(block.1) <- all.par.names
    out <- rbind(out, block.1)
    rm(post.1)
    rm(post.2)
    gc()
    print(paste("Subsample", i, "of", n.loops))
  }
  out_fix <- as.matrix(out[, grep(paste(fix_samp_names, collapse="|"),
                                  colnames(out))])
  colnames(out_fix) <- fix_samp_names
  out_fit <-  matrix(NA, 1, 1)
  random_samples <- list()
  for(i in 1:length(random_samp_names)){
    random_samples[[i]] <- out[, grep(random_samp_names[i], colnames(out))]
  }
  names(random_samples) <- random_samp_names
  out_lst1 <- list(fixed_samples=out_fix,
                   random_samples=random_samples,
                   fitted_samples=out_fit)
  return(out_lst1)
}
post_ss <- 10000
post1 <- inla.posterior.sampler(inl1, full.ss=post_ss, part.ss=post_ss/2)

# *******************    here is the important part    *************************
# get posterior mean slope for the subset cells along with 95% CrI using the
# posterior samples. this is standard practice, right?
(m1 <- mean(apply(post1$random_samples$random_slopes[,subset], 1, mean)))
(sd1 <- sd(apply(post1$random_samples$random_slopes[,subset], 1, mean)))
(cl1 <- quantile(apply(post1$random_samples$random_slopes[,subset], 1, mean),
                 probs=c(0.025, 0.975)))

# is it possible to use the posterior means and SD for each cell in the
# subset, along with monte carlo simulation, to get the mean slope for the
# subset, along with something like a 95% CI?
sims <- post_ss
post_means_and_sds <- cbind(grid1$rand_slopes_mean[subset],
                            grid1$rand_slopes_sd[subset])
simulation_mat1 <- matrix(NA, nrow=max(subset), ncol=sims)
for(i in 1:max(subset)){
  simulation_mat1[i,] <- rnorm(sims, mean=post_means_and_sds[i,1],
                               sd=post_means_and_sds[i,2])
}
(m2 <- mean(apply(simulation_mat1, 2, mean)))
(sd2 <- sd(apply(simulation_mat1, 2, mean)))
(cl2 <- quantile(apply(simulation_mat1, 2, mean), probs=c(0.025, 0.975)))

# compare posterior sampling approach and monte carlo approach
data.frame(subsetmean=c(m1, m2), sd=c(sd1, sd2), lcl=c(cl1[1], cl2[1]),
           ucl=c(cl1[2], cl2[2]), row.names=c("posterior", "montecarlo"))

# why the difference? is the monte carlo estimate tighter because it doesn't
# take into account other uncertainties (covariance, spatial structure)? is
# there a way to use other parts of the inla output to fix this?

VEGTYPEB = the factor for the binary component

	~ ... + VEGTYPEB + ...

that is the names you need to use in the lincomb

an alternative, is to use

	f(VEGTYPEB, model="iid",
		hyper = list(prec = list(initial = -3, fixed=TRUE))))

which will give a vector of results, and then the code above might
work.

be aware, that the factor as a fixed effect will remove a reference
level (like lm(), unless you request otherwise), which the f()
approach will not. maybe you need to add constr=T in the f().

Hi Tim,

to add to Haakon's suggestions, item 1. can be skipped if you have
space to store all the configs (which I think you already do).
The configs (that store the information about each numerical
integration component for the posterior mixture distribution arising
from the computations) are used by inla.posterior.sample. In the
"excursions" package, we use them for a sampling method tailored to
computing posterior event probabilities, in a way that can take
skewness (and other) corrections into account, that I believe the
current inla.posterior.sample implementation doesn't (but this may get
implemented in the future).

However, none of that really solves the issue of needing to store lots
and lots of samples.
The good news is that there are partial solutions available, and more
coming in the future.
1. For posterior means and variances, you don't need access to all the
samples at the same time; you can instead accumulate the needed
information from a sequence of sample batches, resulting in the same
result as when first generating all the samples and then summarising
them.
2. For quantiles, you could use sample batches and apply a recursive
quantile estimator. This will not be as accurate (for a given sample
size) as quantiles from the full sample, but it massively reduces the
storage requirements; by producing more samples in total, you
effectively trade storage space for computation time.
3. One of my ongoing projects is a Bayesian improvement of the
recursive technique from 2.

Finn

Hi Håvard,

Hi,

Thank you for your response, it has been very useful.
I have simulated some data to run a two likelihoods model and check if I correctly interpreted your response in terms of limcomb syntax, and the outcomes seem to be the expected ones.

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(2345)

# continuous predictor
x <- rnorm(400, mean = 0, sd = 2)

# binomial component
XmatF <- model.matrix(~1+x)
coefB <- c(0.5, 2)
fixedEffects <- matrix(coefB,2,1)

n.groups <- 4
n.sample <- 100
n <- n.groups * n.sample
RFB <- gl(n = n.groups, k = 100,length = n)
XmatR <- model.matrix(~RFB:x-1)
coefBR <- rnorm(4, mean = 0, sd = 2.5)
raneffects <- matrix(coefBR,4,1)

lin.predB <- XmatF %*% fixedEffects + XmatR %*% raneffects
binomResponse <- plogis(lin.predB)

# gamma component
XmatF <- model.matrix(~1+x)
coefG <- c(-3.5, -2)
fixedEffects <- matrix(coefG,2,1)

n.groups <- 4
n.sample <- 100
n <- n.groups * n.sample
RFG <- gl(n = n.groups, k = 100,length = n)
XmatR <- model.matrix(~RFG:x-1)
coefGR <- rnorm(4, mean = 0, sd = 4)
raneffects <- matrix(coefGR,4,1)

lin.predG <- XmatF %*% fixedEffects + XmatR %*% raneffects
gammaResponse <- exp(lin.predG)

# inla model
data <- data.frame(binomResponse = c(binomResponse,rep(NA,400)),
        gammaResponse = c(rep(NA,400),gammaResponse),
        interceptB = c(rep(1,400),rep(NA,400)), interceptG = c(rep(NA,400),rep(1,400)),
        xB = c(x,rep(NA,400)), xG = c(rep(NA,400),x),
        RFB = c(as.numeric(RFB),rep(NA,400)), RFG = c(rep(NA,400), as.numeric(RFG)+4))

formulaHURDLE <- data[,c(1:2)] ~ 0 + interceptB + interceptG + xB + xG + f(RFB,xB, model = 'iid') + f(RFG, xG, model = 'iid')

lcsB <- inla.make.lincombs(RFB = diag(4),
        xB = rep(1, 4))
lcsG <- inla.make.lincombs(RFG = diag(4),
        xG = rep(1, 4))
names(lcsG) <- paste(names(lcsB), "G", sep = "")

mod <- inla(formulaHURDLE, data = data,

            family = c("binomial","gamma"),Ntrials = 1,control.family(list(control.link(list(model=c('logit','log')))))

            ,verbose = T,control.predictor=list(link=c(rep(1,400),rep(2,400)))
            ,lincomb = c(lcsB, lcsG))

summary(mod)

print("LinComb BINOMIAL"); inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.lincomb.derived$lc1)
print("LinComb BINOMIAL manually calculated"); (inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.fixed$xB) + inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.random$RFB$index.1))

print("LinComb GAMMA"); inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.lincomb.derived$lc1G)
print("LinComb GAMMA manually calculated"); (inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.fixed$xG) + inla.emarginal(function(x) x, mod$marginals.random$RFG$index.1))
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I have checked the approach suggested by you (not to include the continuous predictor outside f() and therefore, not to use the limcomb argument) and the results match those above.

Finally, I have another question. How to estimate the percentage of variance explained by the random factor respect to the total variance of the model?. Does it make sense to use the approach proposed here <https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/full/10.1098/rsif.2017.0213> to get the observation-level variance of binomial and gamma variables? How could such an approach apply by using INLA?

Thank you!

Juanmi

I have noticed this as well with binomial models, not so much in that it produces worse results (sometimes they are better) but that supplying different initial values frequently results in a different posterior than sticking with the defaults.  Both are often good, but they are nonetheless different.  On the one hand, no matter where you start, the results seem to be repeatable from that starting point, so that is good.  On the other hand, it would nice if initial values only affected optimization time (which is what I had assumed) rather than the result.  It’s almost  as if finding the mode in high dimensions can be tricky!

Perhaps the solution is tightening the tolerance criteria as H suggests.  Of course, we don’t want that to slow things down too much either.  Perhaps there is a happy medium.  I will give that a try.

On a separate but perhaps related note, the initial value seems to make all the difference with the experimental robit link (thank you again for adding that) but I suspect that is because that link is tricky to estimate and part of the specification may just involve working backward from a good initial estimate.

posterior and then the optimizer have some issues finding the mode.

If this is a 'feature' of the model, then I usually do

                r = inla(...)

to make sure its stable. You can also increase the accuracy in the

inner optimization, like

                control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-10)

If you do not expect a flat posterior, then tighting the model in

terms of more informative priors will do wonders.

xX = xLatent[idxX,]

xTime08[,i]=simdata[[i]]$latent[idxTime+addd[k]]}

      brks = floor(seq(0, nrow(Xp), length.out = nBatch+1))
        for(batch in 1:nBatch){

y[,j]<-rpois(nrow(lambda2),lambda=lambda2[,j])}

  }

        # Calculate predictions

thanks for looking into this.

I was not expecting a very flat prior because the model was constrained for
several other data-sets. However, the "r2 <- inla.rerun(r)" took nearly more than 40 minutes
longer than the original fit. And indeed, both theta and x changed quite
a bit. So its unstable for this specific data-set.

m = get("inla.models", INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv());m$latent$rw1$min.diff
<- 1e-6; assign("inla.models", m, INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())

yes, reducing tolerance and using the

	r = inla.rerun(r)

feature, are my best guesses.

In some cases, tuning initial values will help. In general, it seems
to be benefitial to start with a very tight model and losen it up,
instead of the other way around.

I must admit, that optimisation problems are often a sign of something
else (!!!!), like a very weakly identified model because of weak data
or a simply to complex model with 'weak' priors...

doing the same thing on a simulated dataset. you may set the
observational variance to be small and fixed, and then any errors you
may do, should be clearly visible. Its often hard to know if a thing

Hi,

I am trying to run a spatio-temporal model on 21 times series. Each time series has different spatial coordinates.
I used the model "dMatern" for spatial correlation and the model "ar" for temporal correlation.
When combining them, I would like to apply a different order p for each time series. I tried to create a vector containing the 21 p values and use them in control.group but I have the feeling that it does not work.
Another concern I have is about overfitting. When I plot fitted values against observed values from the model with only spatial correlation, I don´t see any overfitting issue (see attached figure). However, when I add the temporal correlation, the model fits almost perfectly the data (see attached figure). Is that an issue?
I would really appreciate your help. I copy my code below.

Thanks in advance.

Regards,

loc <- as.matrix(cbind(coord$x, coord$y)) # Matrix of 21 coordinates.

#Spatial model
f1 <- xs ~
  -1 + 1 +
  crust + season + # Categorical variables
  swc.std + ts.std + # Quantitative variables
  swc.std:ts.std + swc.std:crust + ts.std:crust + #Interactions
  f(replicate, # replicate is an index from 1 to 21 to identify each time series
    model = "dmatern",
    locations = loc)

I1 <- inla(f1,
           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
           family = "gamma",
           data = dat,
           verbose = TRUE)

v2 = c(2,1,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,3,4,5,2,4,4,3,3,3,1) # Vector of 21 orders p for the AR processes

#Spatio-temporal model

  -1 + 1 +
  crust + season +
  swc.std + ts.std +
  swc.std:ts.std + swc.std:crust + ts.std:crust +
  f(replicate,
    model = "dmatern",
    locations = loc,
    group = day, # From 1 to 730 (each time series has 730 days)
    control.group = list(model = "ar", order = v2))

I2 <- inla(f2,
           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
           family = "gamma",
           data = dat,
           verbose = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to make sense of the interpolator options available as part of the control.inla command.  Looking over the literature, I have seen the following options for deriving the marginal distribution of the hyper parameters

1.  Gaussian approximation
2.  Laplace approximation
3.  Numeric integration using a new regular grid
4.  Interpolation using existing points on a regular grid
5.  Asymmetric Gaussian interpolation
6.  Integration-free

I'm trying to understand how 1-6 correspond to the options in control.inla.  I assume that (a) gaussian corresponds to Gaussian approximation, that (b) nearest, quadratic, and weighted.distance correspond to alternative approaches to interpolation using existing regular grid points, and that (c) ccdintegrate corresponds to asymmetric Gaussian interpolation.

This raises the following questions:

1.  Are points a, b, and c correct?
2.  Is integration-free the default?  It sounds like it, but this doesn't seem to appear in the documentation, which simply says that "auto" is the default.
3.  I would assume that gridsum implies numerical integration on a regular grid, but I think that getting accurate results requires a bigger and finer grid than the one used if we simply need to integrate out the hyper parameters en route to the latent parameters.
4.  What does the ccd option for interpolation in control.inla do?
5.  Is the Laplace approach left out entirely?

Any help would be much appreciated.

Sorry for late reply.

A lot of these options are less interesting, and was added when trying
to solve this problem. There is some more historical background for it,
in the INLA-review paper and the working solution is in the 'New
Features' paper.

The truth is that this took a long time to solve, and to figure out how
to do this both quick and robust. What mention in the original INLA
paper does not work well enough, as the numerical integration becomes
to costly to make it robust enough. Essentially, only two options works
well enough (quick and robust),

- explore the grid of hyperparameter values without rotations. then
numerical integration is just a sum over various columns.

- the integration free techniquie in the 'new features' article.

the first one, is implementen in inla.hyparpar(), like

r = inla(...)
r = inla.hyperpar(r)

and works well in low dimensions, like 2-5, say.

the other one, is the default for dimension >= 2, and use the
integration free approach

all this is for computing marginals for each of the hyperparameters

Let me know if you need more

H

oooh, that is two different things.

for the numerical integration of the hyperparameters, then the
(adaptive) grid is used in dim(theta) <= 2, wheras CCD is used for
dim(theta) >= 3.

for the computation of the marginals for each hyperparameter \theta_i,
then the integration-free approach (see 'New features article') is
used. the grid-approach (without rotation) is used when
inla.hyperpar(result) is used.

subset_fData$small <- as.numeric(subset_fData$size == 1)
